lessons.expl:
·אי הכי רישא…QuestionWestwood · May 7, 2012 · 19:44
① The Braisa regarding the fall and dew on fruits. And they're becoming prepared to accept Tumah … The Braisa says:
Ⅰ The beginning of the Braisa:
The owner discovers the dew on the fruits while they are still wet … and he is pleased … The fruits are made into a ready state to accept Tumah.
Ⅱ The end of the Braisa:
If the owner discovers the fruits after the dew already dried … even if he is pleased … The fruits do not become prepared to accept Tumah.
② In order that the end of the Braisa should not be a challenge to Rava, who holds, regarding giving up hope, that a later mindset can count for before … The Gemara had said that the reason for the end of the Braisa, as to why the fruits do not become ready for Tumah, is not because a later mindset cannot help for before.
③ But rather, because the word written in the Torah that governs this halacha is written:
"יתן — he will put"
④ Since dew false passively, the fruits do not qualify to become prepared to accept Tumah.
⑤ On this the Gemara now asks:
If this reason is correct, dew should never prepare fruits for accepting Tumah, since it is always placed on the fruits passively.
⑥ Yet, in the first part of the Braisa, where the owner discovered the dew while it was still on the fruit, the fruits do become prepared to accept Tumah.
⑦ Therefore, the reason for the end of the Braisa can only be because we need a prior mindset of the owner being pleased with the dew being on the fruit.
⑧ And, a later mindset does not help for before.
⑨ Therefore, the question on Rava comes back.

lessons.title: Rav Pappa's answer, explained, part 1
lessons.chapter: Dew on the fruit
lessons.text: This lesson is his explanation of the step. The Hebrew words and his translation are in the previous lesson’s word sheet.
lessons.expl:
·בעינן כי יותן…AnswerWestwood · May 16, 2012 · 38:15
① The pasuk, which talks about liquid preparing produce to be in a ready state to accept Tumah, says:
"When it will be put."
② The language of the pasuk seems to indicate that even if the liquid is placed on the produce passively, it prepares the produce to accept Tumah.
③ However, even though the word in the pasuk for placing is read in a way that indicates passive is enough, however, the word is written:
"When he will put."
Indicating that active placing of liquid is required.
④ The Gemara now concludes with the explanation of Rav Papa, who resolves this issue.
⑤ Passive placing of liquid is enough.
⑥ However, the passive placing of liquid must be similar to where the owner actively put the liquid on the produce.
⑦ Ⓐ Just as when liquid is placed actively, the owner is aware and pleased.
Ⓑ So, too, even if the liquid is placed passively, the owner must be aware and pleased.
⑧ Therefore:
Ⓐ Dew qualifies as a liquid, even though it is placed passively.
Ⓑ But only on the condition that the owner is aware and pleased.
Ⓒ Therefore, if the produce is still wet with dew, it is as if the dew is being placed with the knowledge of the owner.
Ⓓ So, if the owner is pleased, it qualifies the fruit.
Ⓔ But if it is already dry, it is not as if he is placing the liquid with knowledge.
Ⓕ Therefore, even if he is pleased, it does not qualify the fruit.
⑨ This entire process applies to preparing fruit to be able to accept Tumah, as is governed by the special wording of the pasuk, which indicates that some kind of placing of liquid is required, and not just mindset.
⑩ However, in general, such as by lost objects, we can still say that even a clear potential mindset can be considered as if it is already there.
⑪ Therefore, the case of the dew is no longer a proof against Rava.
lessons.take:
Key takeaway

Dew qualifies as a liquid, even though it is placed passively. But only on the condition that the owner is aware and pleased.

·בעינן כי יותן…AnswerWestwood · May 16, 2012 · 38:15
① The pasuk, which talks about liquid preparing produce to be in a ready state to accept Tumah, says:
"When it will be put."
② The language of the pasuk seems to indicate that even if the liquid is placed on the produce passively, it prepares the produce to accept Tumah.
③ However, even though the word in the pasuk for placing is read in a way that indicates passive is enough, however, the word is written:
"When he will put."
Indicating that active placing of liquid is required.
④ The Gemara now concludes with the explanation of Rav Papa, who resolves this issue.
⑤ Passive placing of liquid is enough.
⑥ However, the passive placing of liquid must be similar to where the owner actively put the liquid on the produce.
⑦ Ⓐ Just as when liquid is placed actively, the owner is aware and pleased.
Ⓑ So, too, even if the liquid is placed passively, the owner must be aware and pleased.
⑧ Therefore:
Ⓐ Dew qualifies as a liquid, even though it is placed passively.
Ⓑ But only on the condition that the owner is aware and pleased.
Ⓒ Therefore, if the produce is still wet with dew, it is as if the dew is being placed with the knowledge of the owner.
Ⓓ So, if the owner is pleased, it qualifies the fruit.
Ⓔ But if it is already dry, it is not as if he is placing the liquid with knowledge.
Ⓕ Therefore, even if he is pleased, it does not qualify the fruit.
⑨ This entire process applies to preparing fruit to be able to accept Tumah, as is governed by the special wording of the pasuk, which indicates that some kind of placing of liquid is required, and not just mindset.
⑩ However, in general, such as by lost objects, we can still say that even a clear potential mindset can be considered as if it is already there.
⑪ Therefore, the case of the dew is no longer a proof against Rava.

·תא שמע דאמר רבי יוחנן…QuestionWestwood · May 30, 2012 · 16:12
① The Gemara now brings another Braisa to resolve the dispute between:
Ⓐ Abaye
Ⓑ And Rava
Regarding the issue of whether prior or actual giving up hope is required for the finder to be permitted to keep the lost object, or potential giving up hope is enough.
② In the Braisa, Rabbi Yochanan says, in the name of Rabbi Yishmael, son of Yehotzadak:
From where do we learn out that an object that became lost to its owner by having been flooded away by a river, that the finder of such an object may keep it?
③ He explains that the pasuk that obligates the finder to return the lost object of his friend says:
"And so you shall do to his donkey, and so you shall do to his garment, and so you shall do to every lost object of your brother, that it shall be lost from him, and you will find it."
④ In the pasuk, when it mentions the lost object, it says:
"It shall be lost from him."
⑤ The words "from him" are extra.
⑥ From this, we learn out: A finder must return a lost object that is lost only from its owner, but the object is accessible to any person.
⑦ This excludes an object lost to its owner through having been flooded away from its owner, since, while it was being lost, it was equally inaccessible to the owner and everyone else.
⑧ Since the Torah excludes it from the obligation to return lost objects, the finder may keep it.

① Regarding an object lost to its owner. There are two cases referred to in the Torah.
Ⓐ One case which is stated openly.
Ⓑ And the other case which is implied.
Ⅰ And the openly stated case:
The object is lost to its owner, but accessible to everyone.
Ⅱ the implied case:
The object was lost to its owner. In a way that it was lost to him and everyone else.

① Rava can say to you:
② Really, the Mishnah is talking about finding a lost object without a sign.

lessons.text: This lesson is his explanation of the step. The Hebrew words and his translation are in the previous lesson’s word sheet.
lessons.expl:
·AnswerWestwood · Nov 26, 2012 · 11:17
The Gemara answers that in the case of the large bundles of wheat that are found in a public place, where the ruling is that the finder must announce them. And that's according to the Braisa… This case can be explained according to both Rabbah and Rava. And each one according to his way of learning.
Ⅰ Rabbah:
① He established the cases of the small bundles of wheat to be speaking about with a sign.
② The Gemara now says that… Rabbah can explain the case of large bundles. Also, to be speaking about with a sign.
(א) Small bundles of wheat with a sign:
Ⓐ In a public place:
ⓐ
ⓑ Because they are likely to be trampled.
ⓒ So the owner is a pessimist. And thinks that they were trampled. So he gives up hope.
Ⓑ In a private place:
ⓐ They are not likely to be trampled.
ⓑ So the owner does not give up hope. And the finder must announce them.
(ב) Large bundles of wheat:
Ⓐ In a public place:
ⓐ They are tall. And thus, not likely to be trampled.
ⓑ Therefore, the owner does not give up hope. And the finder must announce them.
Ⓑ In a private place:
Since they have a sign. The finder must announce them.
Ⅱ Rava:
① He established the cases of the small bundles of wheat to be speaking about without a sign.
② The Gemara now says that Rava can explain the case of large bundles of wheat also to be talking about without a sign.
(inserted under Rava ②) because the place is. The place can be the sign. Place can be a sign.
(א) Small bundles of wheat without a sign:
Ⓐ In a public place:
ⓐ The finder can keep them.
ⓑ Since they get kicked around. The place is not considered to be a reliable sign.
Ⓑ In a private place:
ⓐ They do not get kicked around.
ⓑ Therefore, the place itself will be the sign.
ⓒ Therefore, the finder must announce it.
(ב) Large bundles of wheat:
Ⓐ In a public place:
ⓐ They are heavy. So, they do not get kicked around.
ⓑ Therefore, the place itself is a good sign.
ⓒ Therefore, the finder must announce it.
Ⓑ In a private place:
ⓐ They are not kicked around.
ⓑ Therefore, the place itself is a good sign.
ⓒ Therefore, the finder must announce it.
